vulnerabilities.details:
### Impact
Due to a non-constant-time implementation, information about the private key is leaked through timing information which is observable over the network. An attacker may be able to use that information to recover the key.

### Patches
The `rsa` v0.10 series includes a migration to `crypto-bigint` and constant-time mitigations recommended in `draft-irtf-cfrg-rsa-guidance`. Upgrading to this release should resolve all known constant-time issues.

### References
This vulnerability was discovered as part of the "[Marvin Attack]", which revealed several implementations of RSA including OpenSSL had not properly mitigated timing sidechannel attacks.

[Marvin Attack]: https://people.redhat.com/~hkario/marvin/
vulnerabilities.summary: Marvin Attack: potential key recovery through timing sidechannels

vulnerabilities.details:
The `zip` crate preserves privileged Unix permission bits (SUID, SGID, and sticky bits) from ZIP `external_attributes` during extraction, instead of masking them to safe permission bits. If a privileged process (for example, `root` in an installer, CI/CD pipeline, or container build) extracts an attacker-controlled ZIP archive using `ZipArchive::extract()` or the stream extraction API, files can be created as setuid-root or setgid. This behavior allows the creation of SUID/SGID files during extraction, which can lead to local privilege escalation depending on the execution environment.

For further details see: https://github.com/zip-rs/zip2/security/advisories/GHSA-vv5m-jxxh-4627
vulnerabilities.summary: Insecure Preservation of SUID/SGID Bits during ZIP Extraction Leading to Potential Privilege Escalation

vulnerabilities.details:
In `zip` 9.0.0-pre2, `ZipArchive::extract` creates a symbolic link from an archive entry after validating only the output entry path. The link target bytes are passed directly to the platform symlink API, so a malicious archive can create an entry inside the destination that resolves to an attacker-chosen path outside it. This behavior was verified on macOS and Linux. On either platform, a subsequent application read or write through that extracted entry accesses the external target with the extracting process's permissions.

For further details see: https://github.com/zip-rs/zip2/security/advisories/GHSA-4v9h-p7m9-rh26
vulnerabilities.summary: zip: `ZipArchive::extract` creates symbolic links whose attacker-controlled targets are outside the destination directory

vulnerabilities.details:
`ZipStreamReader::extract()` applies Unix permissions through extracted symlinks without validating the symlink target stays within the destination

For further details see: https://github.com/zip-rs/zip2/security/advisories/GHSA-4684-h2q9-2vcp
vulnerabilities.summary: ZipStreamReader::extract() and ZipArchive::extract() apply Unix permissions through symlinks without confining the target

vulnerabilities.details:
`ZipArchive::extract()` sizes the symlink-target buffer from the uncompressed
size declared in the central directory record, before reading a single byte of
entry data:

```rust
let mut target = Vec::with_capacity(file.size() as usize);
```

Both inputs are attacker-controlled. `ZipFile::size()` returns
`uncompressed_size` verbatim from the central directory, widened to a full `u64`
by a ZIP64 extended-information extra field, and is never cross-checked against
the compressed size, the remaining archive length, or any platform-appropriate
bound for a symlink target. `ZipFile::is_symlink()` is decided entirely by the
`S_IFLNK` bit of the external-attributes field.

`Vec::with_capacity()` is infallible: when the reservation is refused it calls
`handle_alloc_error()` and aborts the process. This is not a Rust panic. It is
not caught by `catch_unwind()`, is unaffected by `panic = "unwind"`, and is not
contained by running the call on a worker thread.

A 112-byte archive is sufficient. One `Stored` entry flagged `S_IFLNK` with a
ZIP64 field declaring `uncompressed_size = 2^62` and a zero-byte payload makes
`extract()` fail with:

```
memory allocation of 4611686018427387904 bytes failed
Aborted (core dumped)          # exit 134
```

The declared value only needs to exceed the host's address space, not its RAM:
`Vec::with_capacity()` maps address space without touching pages, so resident
memory stays flat and the abort happens on the refused reservation itself. Under
a `ulimit -v` cap or a memory-constrained container the threshold drops far
enough that a plain 32-bit `uncompressed_size` with no ZIP64 field suffices.

Applications that extract archives from untrusted input are affected on Unix and
Windows targets with default features and no special configuration: upload
handling, mail-attachment processing, package and artefact ingestion, backup
restore and container-image layer extraction. No confidentiality or integrity
property is affected: there is no memory unsafety, no out-of-bounds access, no
disclosure and no data corruption.

The fix landed in [zip-rs/zip2#984](https://github.com/zip-rs/zip2/pull/984) and
shipped in 9.0.0.

For further details see: https://github.com/zip-rs/zip2/security/advisories/GHSA-q7v9-x93c-xqv3
vulnerabilities.summary: zip: `ZipArchive::extract` aborts the process on a symlink entry with a large declared size
zip: AES Entry HMAC Authentication Bypass on Premature EOF
zip: legacy Shrink/Reduce/Implode decoder: denial of service from attacker-controlled ZIP64 uncompressed size
zip: Arbitrary file write outside the extraction directory, because ZipArchive::extract validates symlink targets lexically.
zip: Critical Parser Differential & Security Control Bypass via Dual-Header Inconsistencies (Zip Cloaking) Leading to Arbitrary File Overwrite & RCE

vulnerabilities.details:
### Summary

The symbolic-link branch of `ZipArchive::extract_internal()` allocates a buffer using an attacker-declared size before reading any entry data. A 112-byte archive terminates the extracting process with `SIGABRT` through this infallible allocation.

### Details

```rust
#[cfg(any(unix, windows))]
if file.is_symlink() {
    let mut target = Vec::with_capacity(file.size() as usize); // @audit unbounded memory allocation
    file.read_to_end(&mut target)?;
    drop(file);
    make_symlink(&outpath, &target, &self.shared.files)?;
    continue;
}
```

[`src/read/mod.rs#L399-L405`](https://github.com/zip-rs/zip2/blob/6f09b3064ec87c3a69ea9f3413f9f9638b4aa446/src/read/mod.rs#L399-L405) (reviewed commit `6f09b306`); the same code is at [`src/read.rs#L417-L418`](https://github.com/zip-rs/zip2/blob/v8.6.0/src/read.rs#L417-L418) in released v8.6.0.

Both inputs are attacker-controlled:

- [`ZipFile::size()`](https://github.com/zip-rs/zip2/blob/6f09b3064ec87c3a69ea9f3413f9f9638b4aa446/src/read/zipfile.rs#L243-L246) returns `uncompressed_size` verbatim from the central directory record. A ZIP64 extended-information extra field widens it to a full `u64` ([`src/read/mod.rs#L619-L625`](https://github.com/zip-rs/zip2/blob/6f09b3064ec87c3a69ea9f3413f9f9638b4aa446/src/read/mod.rs#L619-L625)). It is never cross-checked against the compressed size, the remaining archive length, or any platform-appropriate bound for a symlink target.
- [`ZipFile::is_symlink()`](https://github.com/zip-rs/zip2/blob/6f09b3064ec87c3a69ea9f3413f9f9638b4aa446/src/read/zipfile.rs#L256-L260) is decided entirely by the central directory's external-attributes field, via the `S_IFLNK` bit.

**Memory allocation failure → uncatchable process abort.** The reservation is sized from the declared `uncompressed_size` before a single byte of the entry is read. `Vec::with_capacity()` is infallible: on allocator refusal it calls `handle_alloc_error()`, which aborts the process. This is not a Rust panic — it is not caught by `catch_unwind()`, is unaffected by `panic = "unwind"`, and is not contained by isolating the call in a worker thread. This was verified by wrapping the call in all three at once; the process still died with exit 134.

The declared value needed is a property of the host's address space, not of reachability. On a 64 GB host with heuristic overcommit, declared sizes from roughly `2^38` upward abort reliably. Sizes at or above `2^63` instead trip `Vec`'s internal capacity check and produce a *catchable* `capacity overflow` panic, so an attacker simply avoids that band. The reproducer declares `2^62`, which exceeds the 47-bit user address space of x86-64 Linux outright and therefore aborts deterministically regardless of installed RAM or overcommit policy. Under a `ulimit -v` cap or a memory-constrained container the threshold drops far enough that a plain 32-bit `uncompressed_size` with no ZIP64 field suffices — a virtual-memory limit lowers the bar rather than mitigating the defect.

This is process termination, not memory exhaustion: `Vec::with_capacity()` only maps address space and never touches pages, so resident memory stays flat and the abort happens on the refused reservation itself, before any byte is read.

### PoC

The reproducer consists of the following `zip` harness and payload. It requires only the `zip` crate; use a standard Base64 decoder to materialise the archive before running it.

```toml
[package]
name = "zip-poc"
version = "0.1.0"
edition = "2021"

[dependencies]
zip = "8.6.0"
```

```rust
use std::{env, fs::File, io::BufReader};

fn main() {
    let archive_path = env::args().nth(1).expect("usage: poc <archive.zip>");
    let outdir = std::env::temp_dir().join("zip-poc");
    std::fs::create_dir_all(&outdir).unwrap();

    let file = File::open(archive_path).unwrap();
    let mut archive = zip::ZipArchive::new(BufReader::new(file)).unwrap();
    let r = archive.extract(&outdir);            // <-- process dies here
    println!("SURVIVED: {:?}", r);
}
```

Save the Base64 payload below as `archive.b64`, remove its whitespace, decode it with a standard Base64 decoder (for example, `base64 -d archive.b64 > archive.zip` on Linux), and run `cargo run --release -- archive.zip`.

**Uncatchable abort — 112 bytes.** One `Stored` entry named `a`; external attributes `0xA1FF0000` (`S_IFLNK|0777`); ZIP64 extra field declaring `uncompressed_size = 2^62`; zero-byte payload. sha256 `0c68c3934f22651a6bd2726f7d58140124b1839196a1d0ae468864cdfda74676`.

```
UEsDBC0AAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAP////8BAAAAYVBLAQItAy0AAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAP//
//8BAAwAAAAAAAAAAAD/oQAAAABhAQAIAAAAAAAAAABAUEsFBgAAAAABAAEAOwAAAB8AAAAAAA==
```

Observed on x86-64 Linux, rustc 1.93.1, release profile, against both the reviewed commit and released v8.6.0:

```
entries=1
memory allocation of 4611686018427387904 bytes failed
Aborted (core dumped)          # exit 134
```

The `SURVIVED` line never prints. Wrapping `extract()` in `catch_unwind` inside a spawned thread with `panic = "unwind"` produces the identical outcome.

### Impact

Applications running on Unix or Windows targets that call `ZipArchive::extract()` on attacker-supplied input are affected, with default features and no special configuration. The malicious 112-byte archive causes an unrecoverable, uncatchable termination of the extracting process, repeatable at will and not mitigable at the call site with `catch_unwind`, a worker thread, or a pre-flight metadata check.

Upload handling, mail-attachment processing, package and artefact ingestion, backup restore and container-image layer extraction all match this pattern. No confidentiality or integrity property is affected: no memory unsafety, no out-of-bounds access, no disclosure and no data corruption.

### Suggested remediation

Before allocating, compare `file.size()` with a documented, platform-appropriate maximum symlink-target length and reject entries that exceed it. Alternatively, replace `Vec::with_capacity()` with fallible `try_reserve()` and return an I/O error when allocation fails. Do not use Linux's `PATH_MAX` as a cross-platform contract.

Apply the allocation fix to `src/read/stream.rs` as defence-in-depth, although its symlink path is currently unreachable because streaming entries have no symlink attributes.

For reference, the crate already applies exactly this defence to another untrusted size on the same path: `ZipArchive::new()` clamps a suspicious `number_of_files` to zero and explicitly rejects an oversized central directory before reserving ([`src/read/zip_archive.rs#L185-L202`](https://github.com/zip-rs/zip2/blob/6f09b3064ec87c3a69ea9f3413f9f9638b4aa446/src/read/zip_archive.rs#L185-L202)). The symlink branch received neither guard. A survey of `Vec::with_capacity` across `src/` finds exactly two sites sized from untrusted input: `src/read/mod.rs:401` and `src/read/stream.rs:73`.
vulnerabilities.summary: zip: Unbounded Symlink-Target Handling Can Abort Or Exhaust Memory During Extraction

vulnerabilities.details:
### Impact

A single request can crash any application using `body-parser` with default options. When a request carries a `Content-Encoding` (for example `gzip`), `body-parser` pipes it into a decompression stream and, after reading the body, leaves that stream piped with no error listener. A payload of one valid compressed frame followed by trailing bytes decodes and the application responds normally, but the trailing bytes then reach the already-finished decoder, which emits an error that is re-thrown as an uncaught exception and terminates the process. No authentication or matching route is required, since parsing runs before routing.

### Patches

Fixed in body-parser 2.4.0 and 1.20.9. Upgrade to one of these versions.

### Workarounds

Pass `inflate: false` to the body-parser middleware if the application does not need to accept compressed request bodies. This rejects encoded requests before any decompression stream is created.
vulnerabilities.summary: body-parser vulnerable to Denial of Service via trailing bytes after a compressed request body

vulnerabilities.details: deepmerge through 4.3.1 contains a prototype poisoning vulnerability in the mergeObject() function that fails to properly validate keys being written to target objects. Attackers can supply malicious source objects in merge operations to inject attacker-controlled properties into the returned object's prototype, causing applications to inherit unintended values when accessing properties without own-property checks.
vulnerabilities.summary: deepmerge mergeObject() allows prototype poisoning of returned objects

vulnerabilities.details:
### Impact

`fast-uri`'s `serialize()`, `normalize()`, and `resolve()`, when called with the non-default option `reference: 'suffix'` on a reference that has no authority, emit a relative reference whose first path segment contains a bare colon without escaping it. RFC 3986 section 3.3 requires the first segment of a `path-noscheme` reference not to contain a colon, precisely because a bare colon makes the string reparse as an absolute URI with a scheme. `fast-uri`'s default serialization escapes that colon, but the suffix path does not.

For example, `normalize('javascript:alert(1)', { reference: 'suffix' })` returns `javascript:alert(1)`, which reparses as a live `javascript:` scheme; `data:` and `vbscript:` behave the same.

Applications that serialize or normalize a relative reference with `reference: 'suffix'` and then treat the result as a URI can turn inert input into a live `javascript:`, `data:`, or `vbscript:` URL (a cross-site scripting vector), and `equal()` can conflate a scheme-bearing reference with a relative one. Exposure is limited to applications that use the non-default `reference: 'suffix'` option.

### Patches

Upgrade to `fast-uri` `2.4.8`, `3.1.9`, or `4.2.3`.

### Workarounds

Do not use the `reference: 'suffix'` option on untrusted input. If suffix output is required, percent-encode a colon in the first path segment of the result before treating it as a URI.
vulnerabilities.summary: fast-uri vulnerable to scheme injection via an unescaped first-segment colon in suffix references

vulnerabilities.details:
### Impact

`fast-uri` percent-decodes the scheme component with the legacy global `unescape()` before validating it, so an input whose decoded scheme is a valid but dangerous token is emitted as a live scheme. RFC 3986 section 3.1 does not allow percent-encoding in a scheme, so no RFC or WHATWG parser treats such input as having that scheme, but `fast-uri` does.

For example, `normalize('%6Aavascript:alert(1)')` returns `javascript:alert(1)`, `resolve('https://a.example/', '%6Aavascript:alert(1)')` returns `javascript:alert(1)`, and `parse('%6Aavascript:alert(1)').scheme` returns `javascript`. The `%uXXXX` form (`%u006Aavascript:`) produces the same result, and `equal('%68ttp://a/', 'http://a/')` returns `true`.

An application that screens dangerous schemes on the raw input and then stores or renders `normalize(input)` or `resolve(base, input)` turns an inert string into an executable `javascript:`, `data:`, or `vbscript:` URL, a stored or reflected cross-site scripting vector in the consuming application. `equal()` also treats an encoded and a plain scheme as the same, which can bypass equality-based allowlists.

### Patches

Upgrade to `fast-uri` `2.4.8`, `3.1.9`, or `4.2.3`.

### Workarounds

Reject input whose scheme part (before the first `:`, and before any `/`, `?`, or `#`) contains `%`. Alternatively, check `parse(x).scheme` against an allowlist after normalization and use that same parsed result rather than the raw string.
vulnerabilities.summary: fast-uri vulnerable to URI scheme spoofing via percent-encoded scheme decoding

vulnerabilities.details:
### Impact

`fast-uri` versions `>= 2.4.2, <= 2.4.7`, `>= 3.1.3, <= 3.1.8`, and `>= 4.0.1, <= 4.2.2` can silently rewrite the host of an HTTP-family URL (`http`, `https`, `ws`, `wss`, or any scheme with `domainHost: true`). For those schemes `canonicalizeHost()` passes the parsed host to the WHATWG `URL` parser and adopts its `.hostname` without checking that the parser read the whole input as a host. RFC 3986 permits `@` inside the host group and the WHATWG parser strips TAB, LF, and CR, so the authority `fast-uri` reports is rewritten by that second parser with no `error` set: data before an `@` is dropped and whitespace is removed.

For example, `fast-uri` parses `http://a@b@evil.example/` to host `evil.example` (dropping the `b` segment), and a host containing a raw TAB, CR, or LF has those characters stripped. `equal()` then treats a whitespace-smuggled host as the same as the clean one, and `resolve()` rewrites the authority the same way.

Applications that use `fast-uri` to enforce host-based policy (denylists, loopback filtering, redirect validation, outbound proxy routing) on one representation, such as the raw input, see a policy/use desync: the canonical host `fast-uri` returns differs from what was checked, and traffic can be steered to an unintended destination.

### Patches

Upgrade to `fast-uri` `2.4.8`, `3.1.9`, or `4.2.3`.

### Workarounds

Reject URIs whose authority contains more than one `@`, or contains TAB, CR, or LF, before calling `fast-uri`. Alternatively, treat any non-empty `parse(x).error` as fatal, and compare hosts only from the same `parse()` result.
vulnerabilities.summary: fast-uri vulnerable to host confusion via unchecked WHATWG host canonicalization

vulnerabilities.details:
### Impact

`fast-uri`'s `normalize()` and `serialize()` apply RFC 3986 dot-segment removal (`remove_dot_segments`) to the path of a relative-path reference. RFC 3986 section 5.2.4 defines that algorithm only for the merged target path during resolution, not for the reference itself, so applied to the reference it drops leading `..` segments and can turn a document-relative reference into a root-relative one.

For example, `normalize('a/../b')` returns `/b` and `normalize('../x')` returns `x`, so `resolve(base, normalize(ref))` points at a different resource than `resolve(base, ref)`, and `equal()` treats distinct references as the same.

Applications that normalize attacker-supplied or user-supplied relative references and then resolve them, or use them as cache, deduplication, or authorization keys, can have a reference escape its intended directory and point at a different resource.

### Patches

Upgrade to `fast-uri` `2.4.8`, `3.1.9`, or `4.2.3`.

### Workarounds

Do not normalize a relative reference before resolving it. Resolve it against the absolute base first, then normalize the absolute result.
vulnerabilities.summary: fast-uri vulnerable to improper path equivalence in relative reference normalization

vulnerabilities.details:
minimatch 10.2.6 contains an attacker-controlled pattern amplification in firstPhasePreProcess() when optimizationLevel >= 2.

researcher: Reid Downing (b1nv0id)
files: 

- src/index.ts: 690-770
- src/index.ts: 780-796

issue:
input-controlled growth of globParts during first-phase preprocessing, followed by quadratic second-phase processing.

the **/../ transformation clones a globparts entry and appends the clone to the same globparts array:
```
parts.splice(gs, 1)
const other = parts.slice(0)
other[gs] = '**'
globParts.push(other)
```
this occurs inside a do...while (didSomething) fixpoint loop, allowing generated entries to be processed again.

the expanded globparts array is subsequently processed by secondPhasePreProcess(), which performs pairwise comparisons:
```
for (let i = 0; i < globParts.length - 1; i++) {
  for (let j = i + 1; j < globParts.length; j++) {
    this.partsMatch(...)
  }
}
```
an attacker who can supply a glob pattern can therefore cause additional pattern entries to be generated during preprocessing, followed by quadratic pairwise processing, resulting in excessive cpu and memory consumption.
vulnerabilities.summary: minimatch has potential denial of service via globparts amplification

vulnerabilities.details:
### Impact

A bad regular expression is generated any time you have two parameters within a single segment, separated by something that is not a period (`.`). For example, `/:a-:b`.

### Patches

For users of 0.1, upgrade to `0.1.10`. All other users should upgrade to `8.0.0`.

These versions add backtrack protection when a custom regex pattern is not provided:

- [0.1.10](https://github.com/pillarjs/path-to-regexp/releases/tag/v0.1.10)
- [1.9.0](https://github.com/pillarjs/path-to-regexp/releases/tag/v1.9.0)
- [3.3.0](https://github.com/pillarjs/path-to-regexp/releases/tag/v3.3.0)
- [6.3.0](https://github.com/pillarjs/path-to-regexp/releases/tag/v6.3.0)

They do not protect against vulnerable user supplied capture groups. Protecting against explicit user patterns is out of scope for old versions and not considered a vulnerability.

Version [7.1.0](https://github.com/pillarjs/path-to-regexp/releases/tag/v7.1.0) can enable `strict: true` and get an error when the regular expression might be bad.

Version [8.0.0](https://github.com/pillarjs/path-to-regexp/releases/tag/v8.0.0) removes the features that can cause a ReDoS.

### Workarounds

All versions can be patched by providing a custom regular expression for parameters after the first in a single segment. As long as the custom regular expression does not match the text before the parameter, you will be safe. For example, change `/:a-:b` to `/:a-:b([^-/]+)`.

If paths cannot be rewritten and versions cannot be upgraded, another alternative is to limit the URL length. For example, halving the attack string improves performance by 4x faster.

### Details

Using `/:a-:b` will produce the regular expression `/^\/([^\/]+?)-([^\/]+?)\/?$/`. This can be exploited by a path such as `/a${'-a'.repeat(8_000)}/a`. [OWASP](https://owasp.org/www-community/attacks/Regular_expression_Denial_of_Service_-_ReDoS) has a good example of why this occurs, but the TL;DR is the `/a` at the end ensures this route would never match but due to naive backtracking it will still attempt every combination of the `:a-:b` on the repeated 8,000 `-a`.

Because JavaScript is single threaded and regex matching runs on the main thread, poor performance will block the event loop and can lead to a DoS. In local benchmarks, exploiting the unsafe regex will result in performance that is over 1000x worse than the safe regex. In a more realistic environment using Express v4 and 10 concurrent connections, this translated to average latency of ~600ms vs 1ms.

### References

* [OWASP](https://owasp.org/www-community/attacks/Regular_expression_Denial_of_Service_-_ReDoS)
* [Detailed blog post](https://blakeembrey.com/posts/2024-09-web-redos/)
vulnerabilities.summary: path-to-regexp outputs backtracking regular expressions

vulnerabilities.details:
### Impact

`.` and `#` are not word delimiters in the tokenizer, so a flat selector such as
`.a.a.a...` reaches `splitWord()` as a single word token carrying n class or id
indexes. Three passes scanned those index arrays linearly for every index,
making the parse O(n^2) in the number of indexes rather than in input length:
`uniqs()`, the `indices.forEach` loop, and the Sass-interpolation filter.
Parsing a 400 KB flat selector took ~34 s on a modern laptop, fully occupying a
single thread. A benign selector of identical byte size parses in tens of
milliseconds, so the cost is driven by the index count, not the input size.
The nesting depth of such a selector is 0, so the `maxNestingDepth` guard added
in 7.1.3 offers no protection.

Reachability is deployment dependent. Only consumers that parse untrusted,
attacker-supplied selectors synchronously in a request path are exposed, for
example CSS sanitizers, CSS-in-JS services and online playgrounds. Ordinary
build-time use on trusted sources is not affected.

### Patches

Fixed in 7.1.6. The three passes now use Set membership tests, making parsing
linear in the number of indexes. There is no behaviour change: parsing is
byte-identical on a differential corpus of 8413 selectors.

### Workarounds

Cap the size of selectors accepted from untrusted sources before parsing.
vulnerabilities.summary: PostCSS: Quadratic complexity in flat selector parsing allows CPU exhaustion

vulnerabilities.details:
### Summary

The `v3()`, `v5()`, and `v6()` [API methods](https://github.com/uuidjs/uuid#api-summary) (not `uuid` release versions) accept external output buffers but do not reject out-of-range writes (small `buf` or large `offset`).  
By contrast, `v4()`, `v1()`, and `v7()` API methods explicitly throw `RangeError` on invalid bounds.

This inconsistency allows **silent partial writes** into caller-provided buffers.


### Affected code

- `src/v35.ts` (`v3()`/`v5()` path) writes `buf[offset + i]` without bounds validation.
- `src/v6.ts` writes `buf[offset + i]` without bounds validation.

### Reproducible PoC

```bash
cd /home/StrawHat/uuid
npm ci
npm run build

node --input-type=module -e "
import {v4,v5,v6} from './dist-node/index.js';
const ns='6ba7b810-9dad-11d1-80b4-00c04fd430c8';
for (const [name,fn] of [
  ['v4()',()=>v4({},new Uint8Array(8),4)],
  ['v5()',()=>v5('x',ns,new Uint8Array(8),4)],
  ['v6()',()=>v6({},new Uint8Array(8),4)],
]) {
  try { fn(); console.log(name,'NO_THROW'); }
  catch(e){ console.log(name,'THREW',e.name); }
}"
```

Observed:

- `v4() THREW RangeError`
- `v5() NO_THROW`
- `v6() NO_THROW`

Example partial overwrite evidence captured during audit:

```text
same true buf [
  170, 170, 170, 170,
   75, 224, 100,  63
]
v6 [
  187, 187, 187, 187,
   31,  19, 185,  64
]
```

### Security impact

- **Primary**: integrity/robustness issue (silent partial output).
- If an application assumes full UUID writes into preallocated buffers, this can produce malformed/truncated/partially stale identifiers without error.
- In systems where caller-controlled offsets/buffer sizes are exposed indirectly, this may become a security-relevant logic flaw.

### Suggested fix

Add the same guard used by `v4()`/`v1()`/`v7()`:

```ts
if (offset < 0 || offset + 16 > buf.length) {
  throw new RangeError(`UUID byte range ${offset}:${offset + 15} is out of buffer bounds`);
}
```

Apply to:

- `src/v35.ts` (covers `v3()` and `v5()`)
- `src/v6.ts`
vulnerabilities.summary: uuid: Missing buffer bounds check in v3/v5/v6 when buf is provided

vulnerabilities.details: Zod schema-validation library through 4.6.5 contains an uncontrolled resource consumption vulnerability that allows attackers to exhaust memory by submitting a large array to an application using an array schema without a length constraint. Attackers can exploit the handleArrayResult parse logic in $ZodArray, which accumulates every validation issue for each failing element with no cap or early termination, causing the process to allocate excessive issue objects and crash due to out-of-memory conditions.
vulnerabilities.summary: Zod can exhaust memory while validating oversized constrained collections
opentelemetry-go: AttributeValueLengthLimit is fully bypassed by attribute values composed of valid U+FFFD runes

vulnerabilities.details:
The golang.org/x/crypto/openpgp package is unsafe by design, has numerous known security issues, is not maintained, and should not be used.

If you are required to interoperate with OpenPGP systems and need a maintained package, consider github.com/ProtonMail/go-crypto/openpgp which is a maintained fork that aims to be a drop-in replacement for this package.
vulnerabilities.summary: The golang.org/x/crypto/openpgp package is unmaintained, unsafe by design, and has known security issues

vulnerabilities.details: Out-of-bounds Read in the send_ssi_file function in civetweb.c in CivetWeb through 1.10 allows attackers to cause a Denial of Service or Information Disclosure via a crafted SSI file.

CivetWeb through 1.16, when built with USE_HTTP2 and enable_http2 on, contains a use-after-free vulnerability in handle_http2() that retains freed :method and :path pointers. Unauthenticated remote attackers can send a later HEADERS frame omitting these pseudo-headers to influence request method or path seen by access rules, or crash the server.
vulnerabilities.summary: CivetWeb through 1.16 HTTP/2 Use-After-Free via Stale Pseudo-Header State
